### Round 2: invoice CSV export

Scope check: 13 of 27 questions registered
Later: the column list, file encoding for the spreadsheet app finance uses, an audit trail of who exported what, how long a ready file stays downloadable

#### Who runs it and what it covers

❓ Q4: **Should the export be available to the finance role only?**

Context:
- The export exists for the finance team's month-end reconciliation (user, round 1).
- The admin page has two roles, support and finance (user, round 1).
- Support staff can see invoice lists but not payment details, meaning the payment information the admin page hides from the support role (user, round 1).
- A file both roles download would either carry payment details to support or need a second, reduced layout (judgment).

➡️ My recommendation: **Yes, finance role only.** Finance is the only stated user of the export. Limiting it to that role keeps payment details away from support without building a second file layout that no one has asked for (verified, user, round 1: the export is for finance's reconciliation and support may not see payment details).
Flips if: support staff also need to download invoice lists for their own work.

Alternatives:
- (b) Both roles; support's file leaves out payment details. Serves support too, but costs a second layout and a per-role test for each column (judgment; origin: new (ours))
- (c) Both roles, the same file. Simplest, but hands support the payment details the page hides from them (user, round 1: support role permissions; origin: new (ours))

---

❓ Q5: **Should one export cover every customer's issued invoices for one chosen calendar month?**

Context:
- Finance closes its books on the calendar month (user, round 1).
- The export is for month-end reconciliation, so one run should match one closed period (user, round 1).
- An issued invoice is one that has been issued; drafts are excluded (user, round 1).
- One month for the largest single customer account is about 40,000 rows, so an all-customer month is larger than that (user, round 1).

➡️ My recommendation: **Yes: pick a calendar month and get every customer's issued invoices for it.** A month-end close reconciles the whole period, not one account, so one file per closed month is the unit finance works in (verified, user, round 1: finance closes its books on the calendar month).
Flips if: finance reconciles one customer account at a time.

Alternatives:
- (b) One customer account for one month. Smaller files, but finance runs it once per customer to close a month (judgment; origin: new (ours))
- (c) Any date range with an optional customer filter. Flexible, but a range can straddle two closed months and the file no longer matches one period (user, round 1: calendar-month close; origin: new (ours))

---

❓ Q6: **Which invoice date places an invoice in a month: its issue date?**

Context:
- Finance closes its books on the calendar month (user, round 1).
- An issued invoice is one that has been issued; drafts are excluded (user, round 1).
- An invoice can carry several dates (issue, due, paid), and each can fall in a different month (judgment).

Withheld: which date finance's ledger uses to put an invoice into a period. Nothing stated so far says, and the answer decides which month every borderline invoice lands in.

Alternatives:
- (a) Issue date. Matches an invoiced-revenue view of the month, but disagrees with a ledger that books on payment (judgment; origin: new (ours))
- (b) Due date. Matches a receivables-ageing view, but an invoice issued on the 30th and due next month moves out of the month it was issued in (judgment; origin: new (ours))
- (c) Payment date. Matches a cash-received view, but unpaid issued invoices drop out of the file entirely (judgment; origin: new (ours))

---

❓ Q7: **In which timezone do the month's boundaries fall?**

Context:
- Finance closes its books on the calendar month (user, round 1).
- Customers are billed in USD, EUR and GBP, so they likely span several timezones (user, round 1; the timezone spread is judgment).
- An invoice issued at 23:30 on the 31st in one timezone is in the next month in another, so the boundary decides which file it is in (judgment).

Withheld: the timezone finance closes its books in, and whether the company has a single accounting timezone. Only finance can say.

Alternatives:
- (a) UTC. Unambiguous and the same for every run, but differs from a local close by up to a day at each boundary (judgment; origin: new (ours))
- (b) The company's accounting timezone. Matches how finance closes the month, but has to be named and kept fixed (judgment; origin: new (ours))
- (c) Each customer's own timezone. Matches the customer's invoice date, but the file no longer covers one consistent period (judgment; origin: new (ours))

---

❓ Q8: **Are invoices issued in the month but later voided or cancelled in the file?**

Context:
- An issued invoice is one that has been issued; drafts are excluded (user, round 1).
- That rule says nothing about an invoice issued and then voided or cancelled (user, round 1).
- Reconciliation compares the file against finance's books, so the file has to treat voids the way the books do (user, round 1: reconciliation purpose; the comparison is judgment).

Withheld: how finance's books record an invoice voided after it was issued. Only finance can say.

Alternatives:
- (a) Included, with a status column. Every issued invoice is visible, but finance has to filter voids out when the books exclude them (judgment; origin: new (ours))
- (b) Excluded. A cleaner file, but an invoice that was issued silently disappears from the month (judgment; origin: new (ours))
- (c) Listed in a separate file. Keeps both views, but finance now reconciles two files per month (judgment; origin: new (ours))

---

❓ Q9: **What does finance reconcile the export against, and which fields do they match on?**

Context:
- The export is for finance's month-end reconciliation (user, round 1).
- The answer decides the column list (a later topic), for example invoice number, customer, issue date, amount, currency, status, payment reference (judgment).

Discovery: what the file is matched against (an accounting ledger, a payment processor's report, a bank statement) and the fields used to match, which sets the columns.

#### Delivering the file

❓ Q10: **Should the person request the export and download it from the page once it is ready, instead of waiting while it builds?**

Context:
- The page's other downloads build the file inside the web request, which times out after 30 seconds (user, round 1).
- One month for the largest single customer account is about 40,000 rows; an all-customer month is larger (user, round 1).
- No one has measured how long a 40,000-row build takes, so whether it fits in 30 seconds is unknown (judgment).
- A timeout at month-end leaves finance with no file at the point they need it (judgment).

➡️ My recommendation: **Yes: request it, then download it from the page when it is ready.** The existing in-request pattern has a hard 30-second limit, and the biggest month for a single account alone is about 40,000 rows. A production export cannot rely on the build finishing inside that limit (verified, user, round 1: in-request downloads time out after 30 seconds; the largest account-month is about 40,000 rows).
Flips if: a measured build of a full all-customer month finishes well under 30 seconds.

Alternatives:
- (b) Wait on the page; the file builds in the request like the other downloads. Matches the existing pattern, but fails at month-end if the month grows past what fits in 30 seconds (user, round 1: 30-second timeout; origin: new (ours))
- (c) Emailed when ready. No page revisit, but puts invoice and payment data in email (judgment; origin: new (ours))

---

❓ Q11: **Should mechanism decisions (job system, file storage, streaming) wait until planning?**

Context:
- Question Q10 (download when ready) above recommends a "ready later" delivery, which implies a mechanism such as a background job and stored files (judgment).
- The page's existing downloads build the file inside the web request, and that pattern is the one planning would extend or replace (user, round 1).
- This interview settles what the export does; planning settles how it is built, unless you want the how settled here (judgment).

➡️ My recommendation: **Yes, settle mechanisms at planning.** The only stated fact about how downloads work today is the in-request build and its 30-second limit. That is enough to set the behavior but not to pick a job system or storage (verified, user, round 1: other downloads build the file inside the web request).
Flips if: you already know which job system or storage the export must use.

Alternatives:
- (b) Settle them now. Planning starts with fewer open choices, but they are chosen before anyone reads how the page's downloads are built (judgment; origin: new (ours))

#### What the file contains

❓ Q12: **Should amounts appear as plain decimal numbers in major units (1234.56) with a separate currency-code column, with no symbols and no currency conversion?**

Context:
- Amounts are stored as integer cents with a currency code (user, round 1).
- Customers are billed in USD, EUR and GBP, so one file mixes three currencies (user, round 1).
- Finance opens exported files in a spreadsheet (user, round 1).
- Converting to one currency would change the amounts finance is reconciling against their books (judgment).

➡️ My recommendation: **Yes: plain decimal major units plus a currency-code column, no symbols, no conversion.** The file mixes three currencies, so each row needs its code, and conversion would change the amounts being reconciled. A plain number column keeps them summable in the spreadsheet (verified, user, round 1: amounts are integer cents with a currency code, billed in USD, EUR and GBP, and opened in a spreadsheet).
Flips if: finance imports the file into a tool that expects integer cents.

Alternatives:
- (b) Raw integer cents plus the currency code. Exact and simple, but every amount has to be divided by 100 in the spreadsheet before it matches the books (user, round 1: stored as integer cents; origin: new (ours))
- (c) Formatted with symbols (€1,234.56). Readable, but the spreadsheet can read the cells as text and stop summing them (judgment; origin: new (ours))

---

❓ Q13: **Should text values a spreadsheet would read as a formula (starting with =, +, - or @) be written so the spreadsheet shows them as text?**

Context:
- Finance opens exported files in a spreadsheet (user, round 1).
- Formula injection (CSV injection) is a cell that starts with =, +, - or @ and that a spreadsheet runs as a formula when the file is opened; customer-entered text such as a name or reference can carry one (documented, unverified: OWASP, https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/CSV_Injection).
- The quality bar is production (user, round 1).

➡️ My recommendation: **Yes, neutralize them.** Finance opens these files in a spreadsheet, and any customer-controlled text field is a way for a formula to run on a finance workstation (documented, unverified: OWASP CSV Injection; user, round 1: files are opened in a spreadsheet).
Flips if: another system also reads the file and needs every text value exactly as stored.

Alternatives:
- (b) Write values unchanged. Exact values, but a malicious customer name runs as a formula when finance opens the file (documented, unverified: OWASP CSV Injection; origin: new (ours))

---

Answer in any order, by number, by topic, or "accept all recommendations".

Is there something else that would change these recommendations?
pass.why: all four decisions asked, the large-export one as built inside the request or outside it once ready, while a separate question defers the build mechanism to planning; each with Context from user facts, a sourced recommendation or Withheld line, and alternatives
